title: The Mpemba Effect: Why Hot Water Can Freeze Faster Than Cold
question: How can hot water sometimes freeze before cold water, when the hot water has to cool down through the cold water's starting temperature first?
summary: Under certain conditions, a container of hot water freezes faster than an otherwise identical container of cold water — a counterintuitive result known since antiquity, rediscovered by a Tanzanian schoolboy in 1963, and still not fully explained by physicists today.
content:
In 1963, a Tanzanian secondary school student named Erasto Mpemba noticed something odd while making ice cream: the hot mix he put in the freezer froze faster than his classmates' cooler mix. His teacher told him this was impossible and mocked him in front of the class. Mpemba didn't let it go. He kept testing it, and eventually a visiting physics professor, Denis Osborne, took him seriously enough to run controlled experiments. They found Mpemba was right, and in 1969 the two published a paper together. The phenomenon now bears his name, though Aristotle, Francis Bacon, and Descartes had all noted versions of it centuries earlier and been dismissed just as readily.

Why This Shouldn't Happen

Basic thermodynamics says hot water must pass through every intermediate temperature on its way to freezing — including the cold water's starting temperature. So how could it possibly arrive at 0°C first? The honest answer is that the effect is real under specific conditions but stubbornly resistant to a single clean explanation, which is part of what makes it such a satisfying puzzle: it sits right at the boundary between "obviously wrong" and "actually happening in front of you."

The Leading Candidate Explanations

Several mechanisms plausibly contribute, and they likely combine rather than compete. Hot water evaporates faster, losing mass and therefore needing less total energy removed to freeze what remains. Hot water can develop stronger convection currents, circulating heat to the surface faster where it radiates away, while cold water often stays more thermally stratified with a cool top layer that insulates the warmer water below. Dissolved gases matter too: heating water drives off dissolved CO2 and air, and gas-poor water may freeze more readily and conduct heat differently than gas-saturated cold water. Frost and ice formation on the container walls can also behave differently — cold water sometimes grows an insulating layer of frost on its container before freezing solid, while hot water's more vigorous convection can prevent that frost from taking hold as effectively.

Why It's Still Contested

A 2016 study by Henry Burridge and Paul Linden attempted to systematically reproduce the effect and found it maddeningly sensitive to setup: thermometer placement, container shape, ambient humidity, and the exact definition of "frozen" (ice forming at the surface versus the whole volume solidifying) could flip results between experiments. Some researchers now argue the "effect" is less a single unified phenomenon than a grab-bag of different physical quirks that occasionally align to produce the same qualitative outcome — hot water winning the race — under a narrow, hard-to-specify band of starting conditions. Others maintain it's real and reproducible if you control variables carefully enough.

A Broader Lesson

Mpemba's story is often told as a parable about intellectual humility: a teenager noticed something his teacher insisted was impossible, and he turned out to be onto something real that had eluded formal scrutiny for centuries. But the deeper lesson may be about the limits of "obvious" physical reasoning. Thermodynamics tells you where a system must end up and bounds how it gets there, but real systems have geometry, convection, evaporation, and impurities that idealized single-variable reasoning routinely ignores. The Mpemba effect is a reminder that "it violates a basic law" and "it violates my simplified mental model of that law" are not the same claim.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamics Perspective
perspectives.description: The effect never violates the laws of thermodynamics themselves — only a naive single-variable model of cooling. Real freezing depends on convection, evaporation, and boundary conditions that idealized textbook problems strip away.

perspectives.title: Experimental Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: The 2016 Burridge-Linden study showed the effect's reproducibility hinges on precise, often unstated experimental parameters, raising the question of whether 'the Mpemba effect' names one phenomenon or several coincidentally overlapping ones.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Aristotle described a version of this phenomenon over two thousand years before Mpemba, and it was dismissed each time it resurfaced — a recurring pattern where authority overrides observation until an outsider insists on the evidence.

perspectives.title: Materials Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Container geometry, frost formation dynamics, and dissolved gas content change the effective thermal conductivity and nucleation behavior of the water, meaning the 'same' liquid in different vessels is not really the same experiment.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The Mpemba effect is a case study in how a phenomenon can be simultaneously real, reproducible in the right conditions, and resistant to a tidy causal explanation — challenging the assumption that science always converges on a single clean mechanism.

The role of anecdote and amateur observation in scientific discovery
openQuestions: Is the Mpemba effect one unified phenomenon or several distinct mechanisms that happen to produce the same result?
Under what precise, reproducible conditions does the effect reliably appear?
Are there analogous 'inverted intuition' effects waiting to be found in other physical systems?
How many real phenomena have been dismissed by authority before amateur persistence forced a second look?
